claim: USP16 was identified among factors captured by mass spectrometry of pre-ribosomal subunits trapped on RIOK1.
source: To identify novel proteins promoting the final maturation of human 40S subunits, we characterized pre-ribosomal subunits trapped on RIOK1 by mass spectrometry, and identified the deubiquitinase USP16 among the captured factors.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that mass spectrometry was performed and USP16 was identified.

claim: USP16 is a component of late cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits.
source: We demonstrate that USP16 constitutes a component of late cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits that promotes the removal of ubiquitin from an internal lysine of ribosomal protein RPS27a/eS31.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on the study's experimental results.

claim: USP16 promotes the removal of ubiquitin from an internal lysine of ribosomal protein RPS27a/eS31.
source: We demonstrate that USP16 constitutes a component of late cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits that promotes the removal of ubiquitin from an internal lysine of ribosomal protein RPS27a/eS31.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this functional role of USP16.

claim: USP16 deletion leads to late 40S subunit maturation defects.
source: USP16 deletion leads to late 40S subunit maturation defects, manifesting in incomplete processing of 18S rRNA and retarded recycling of late-acting ribosome biogenesis factors, revealing an unexpected contribution of USP16 to the ultimate step of 40S synthesis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the phenotype observed upon USP16 deletion.

claim: USP16 deletion manifests in incomplete processing of 18S rRNA.
source: USP16 deletion leads to late 40S subunit maturation defects, manifesting in incomplete processing of 18S rRNA and retarded recycling of late-acting ribosome biogenesis factors, revealing an unexpected contribution of USP16 to the ultimate step of 40S synthesis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a manifestation of USP16 deletion.

claim: USP16 deletion leads to retarded recycling of late-acting ribosome biogenesis factors.
source: USP16 deletion leads to late 40S subunit maturation defects, manifesting in incomplete processing of 18S rRNA and retarded recycling of late-acting ribosome biogenesis factors, revealing an unexpected contribution of USP16 to the ultimate step of 40S synthesis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this phenotype.

claim: Ubiquitination of RPS27a appears to depend on active translation.
source: Finally, ubiquitination of RPS27a appears to depend on active translation, pointing at a potential connection between 40S maturation and protein synthesis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: Ribosomes catalyze the synthesis of proteins by reading a messenger RNA (mRNA) template.
source: Ribosomes stand at the center of translation in all kingdoms of life, catalyzing the synthesis of proteins by reading a messenger RNA (mRNA) template.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ribosome function.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis encompasses the action of more than 200 non-ribosomal proteins.
source: Ribosome biogenesis encompasses the action of more than 200 non-ribosomal proteins, so-called assembly or trans-acting factors that collectively ensure that the two ribosomal subunits, a small 40S and a large 60S subunit in eukaryotes, are correctly assembled.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Eukaryotic ribosomes consist of a small 40S and a large 60S subunit.
source: Ribosome biogenesis encompasses the action of more than 200 non-ribosomal proteins, so-called assembly or trans-acting factors that collectively ensure that the two ribosomal subunits, a small 40S and a large 60S subunit in eukaryotes, are correctly assembled.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic ribosome structure.

claim: The initial steps of eukaryotic ribosome synthesis occur in the nucleolus.
source: While the initial steps of eukaryotic ribosome synthesis leading to the formation of immature pre-ribosomal subunits occur in the nucleolus, ribosomal subunits gain competence for protein translation only during their ultimate maturation in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular location of ribosome biogenesis steps.

claim: Ribosomal subunits gain competence for protein translation during their ultimate maturation in the cytoplasm.
source: While the initial steps of eukaryotic ribosome synthesis leading to the formation of immature pre-ribosomal subunits occur in the nucleolus, ribosomal subunits gain competence for protein translation only during their ultimate maturation in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome maturation.

claim: Early cytoplasmic pre-40S particles contain at least eight trans-acting factors in both yeast and human cells.
source: Early cytoplasmic pre-40S particles contain a similar set of at least eight trans-acting factors in both yeast and human cells, namely ENP1, LTV1, casein kinase 1/Hrr25, RRP12, TSR1, the protein kinase and ATPase RIOK2, the endonuclease NOB1, and DIM2/PNO1 (partner of NOB1) (Ameismeier et al., 2018; Ferreira-Cerca et al., 2012; Ghalei et al., 2015; Granneman et al., 2010; Hector et al., 2014; Heuer et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2017; Larburu et al., 2016; Merl et al., 2010; Mitterer et al., 2019; Oeffinger et al., 2004; Scaiola et al., 2018; Schäfer et al., 2006; Schäfer et al., 2003; Strunk et al., 2011; Wyler et al., 2011; Zemp et al., 2014; Zemp et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The endonuclease NOB1 is associated with pre-40S subunits just prior to the final processing of the 3' end of 18S rRNA.
source: Only few trans-acting factors have been found associated with pre-ribosomal subunits just prior to the final processing of the 3' end of 18S rRNA (Fatica et al., 2003; Pertschy et al., 2009; Preti et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2013). In addition to the endonuclease NOB1, these include DIM2 and the protein kinase RIOK1 (Ameismeier et al., 2018; Hector et al., 2014; Turowski et al., 2014; Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DIM2 and RIOK1 are associated with pre-ribosomal subunits just prior to the final processing of the 3' end of 18S rRNA.
source: Only few trans-acting factors have been found associated with pre-ribosomal subunits just prior to the final processing of the 3' end of 18S rRNA (Fatica et al., 2003; Pertschy et al., 2009; Preti et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2013). In addition to the endonuclease NOB1, these include DIM2 and the protein kinase RIOK1 (Ameismeier et al., 2018; Hector et al., 2014; Turowski et al., 2014; Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ATPase activity of RIOK1 is required for rRNA cleavage.
source: The ATPase activity of RIOK1 is required for rRNA cleavage and the eventual dissociation of NOB1 and DIM2 from the subunit (Ferreira-Cerca et al., 2014; Turowski et al., 2014; Vanrobays et al., 2001; Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ATPase activity of RIOK1 is required for the eventual dissociation of NOB1 and DIM2 from the subunit.
source: The ATPase activity of RIOK1 is required for rRNA cleavage and the eventual dissociation of NOB1 and DIM2 from the subunit (Ferreira-Cerca et al., 2014; Turowski et al., 2014; Vanrobays et al., 2001; Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Release or repositioning of DIM2 has been suggested to be necessary for rRNA cleavage and formation of the 40S subunit decoding site.
source: Based on recent structural studies, release or repositioning of DIM2 has been suggested to be necessary for both rRNA cleavage and formation of the 40S subunit decoding site (Ameismeier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural studies.

claim: Pre-40S subunits can be detected in polysome fractions.
source: Although it is generally assumed that immature 40S subunits cannot engage in translation initiation, several studies have shown that pre-40S subunits can be detected in polysome fractions (Belhabich-Baumas et al., 2017; Ferreira-Cerca et al., 2005; García-Gómez et al., 2014; Granneman et al., 2005; Lacombe et al., 2009; Pertschy et al., 2009; Soudet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Pre-40S particles have been shown to associate with mature 60S subunits generating an 80S-like particle in S. cerevisiae.
source: In a so-called 'translation-like cycle', pre-40S particles have been shown to associate with mature 60S subunits generating a so-called 80S-like particle, which might be part of a final proofreading mechanism for 40S subunits (Ferreira-Cerca et al., 2014; García-Gómez et al., 2014; Ghalei et al., 2017; Turowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The existence of an 80S-like particle involved in pre-40S proofreading has not been described in human cells.
source: While cytoplasmic events of 40S subunit maturation in human and yeast are presumed to be highly similar with few functional differences (Badertscher et al., 2015; Carron et al., 2011; Wild et al., 2010; Wyler et al., 2011; Zorbas et al., 2015), the existence of an 80S-like particle involved in pre-40S proofreading has not been described in human cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: USP16 was originally identified as a DUB for histone H2A by biochemical fractionation of HeLa cell extracts.
source: Originally, USP16 (also called Ubp-M) was identified as a DUB for histone H2A by biochemical fractionation of HeLa cell extracts (Cai et al., 1999; Joo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Usp16 is essential for embryonic development of mice.
source: Notably though, Usp16 is essential for embryonic development of mice (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RIOK1 is part of the methylosome that methylates Sm proteins during snRNP biogenesis.
source: As RIOK1 is also part of the methylosome that methylates Sm proteins during snRNP biogenesis (Guderian et al., 2011), the methylosome components PRMT5 and MEP50 were strongly enriched on RIOK1 (Figure 1A and B, Supplementary file 2), as previously reported (Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The methylosome components PRMT5 and MEP50 were strongly enriched on RIOK1.
source: As RIOK1 is also part of the methylosome that methylates Sm proteins during snRNP biogenesis (Guderian et al., 2011), the methylosome components PRMT5 and MEP50 were strongly enriched on RIOK1 (Figure 1A and B, Supplementary file 2), as previously reported (Widmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B and citations to prior research.

claim: 40S ribosomal proteins and the known 40S trans-acting factors DIM2, NOB1 and TSR1 were preferentially isolated with RIOK1(kd) particles.
source: While the methylosome complex was enriched on WT and mutant RIOK1 to a similar extent, 40S ribosomal proteins (RPs) and the known 40S trans-acting factors DIM2, NOB1 and TSR1 were preferentially isolated with RIOK1(kd) particles (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: OTUD6B, G3BP1, and USP16 were the most significant top scorers among proteins enriched on the kinase-dead version of RIOK1.
source: In addition to ribosomal proteins and known 40S trans-acting factors, a number of proteins not previously linked to 40S subunit maturation were found to be strongly enriched on the kinase-dead version of RIOK1, with OTUD6B, G3BP1, and USP16 being the most significant among the top scorers (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: OTUD6B is a deubiquitinase suggested to associate with and deubiquitinate components of the 48S translation pre-initiation complex.
source: OTUD6B is a deubiquitinase (DUB) suggested to associate with and deubiquitinate components of the 48S translation pre-initiation complex, thereby regulating protein synthesis (Sobol et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: G3BP1 is a core component of stress granules and has been linked to diverse aspects of mRNA metabolism.
source: G3BP1 is a core component of stress granules and has been linked to diverse aspects of mRNA metabolism (reviewed in Alam and Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: USP16 has been implicated in the regulation of gene expression, cell cycle progression, differentiation, and the DNA damage response.
source: Lastly, USP16 has originally been described as a DUB of histone H2A and subsequently been implicated in the regulation of gene expression, cell cycle progression, differentiation, and the DNA damage response (Cai et al., 1999; Gu et al., 2016; Joo et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The increased gene dosage of USP16 has been linked to the manifestation of Down's syndrome.
source: Interestingly, the increased gene dosage of USP16, which is located on human chromosome 21, has been linked to the manifestation of Down's syndrome (Adorno et al., 2013), whereas virus-induced downregulation of USP16 has been suggested to be a critical step in tumorigenicity of Hepatitis B virus (Qian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Virus-induced downregulation of USP16 has been suggested to be a critical step in tumorigenicity of Hepatitis B virus.
source: Interestingly, the increased gene dosage of USP16, which is located on human chromosome 21, has been linked to the manifestation of Down's syndrome (Adorno et al., 2013), whereas virus-induced downregulation of USP16 has been suggested to be a critical step in tumorigenicity of Hepatitis B virus (Qian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: USP16 was enriched in all purified 40S particles to an extent comparable to NOB1.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that USP16 was enriched in all purified 40S particles to an extent comparable to NOB1, but was absent in a pull-down of HASt-tagged GFP used as negative control.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from the experiment.

claim: USP16 co-migrated with LTV1, NOB1 and RPS3/uS3 in the 40S peak fractions of sucrose gradients.
source: Consistent with the assumption that USP16 is associated with pre-40S particles, USP16 co-migrated with LTV1, NOB1 and RPS3/uS3 in the 40S peak fractions but was enriched neither in the 60S peak nor in heavier fractions.
evidence: This is based on sucrose gradient data from the experiment.

claim: Both USP16(WT)- and USP16(C205S)-StHA localized to the cytoplasm.
source: First, to determine their subcellular localization, we transfected these constructs into HeLa cells and observed that both USP16(WT)- and USP16(C205S)-StHA localized to the cytoplasm (Figure 2A) as described previously (Cai et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: USP16-StHA did not accumulate in the nucleus upon treatment of cells with leptomycin B.
source: In contrast, USP16-StHA did not accumulate in the nucleus upon treatment of cells with LMB (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: USP16 must be associated with a cytoplasmic but not a nuclear pool of (pre-)40S particles.
source: Since USP16 is localized to the cytoplasm at steady-state and seems not to shuttle into the nucleus, we conclude that USP16 must be associated with a cytoplasmic but not a nuclear pool of (pre-)40S particles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data and LMB treatment results.

claim: Among the main hits in USP16 affinity purification, many 40S RPs were identified along with characterized 40S trans-acting factors known to be associated with cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits.
source: Interestingly, among the main hits we identified many 40S RPs along with characterized 40S trans-acting factors known to be associated with cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits such as ENP1, LTV1, TSR1, DIM2, and NOB1.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data from USP16 affinity purification.

claim: Only few 40S trans-acting factors known to associate with nuclear pre-40S particles or 60S trans-acting factors were identified in USP16 affinity purification and these were co-purified much less efficiently.
source: In contrast, only few 40S trans-acting factors known to associate with nuclear pre-40S particles (e.g. NOC4L, NOP14) or 60S trans-acting factors (e.g. PES1, NOG2) were identified and these were co-purified much less efficiently (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Pre-40S subunits were co-purified with both WT and mutant USP16-StHA as indicated by the presence of NOB1 and RPS3/uS3.
source: This confirmed that pre-40S subunits were co-purified with both WT and mutant USP16-StHA as indicated by the presence of the late 40S trans-acting factor NOB1 and the 40S RP RPS3/uS3, whereas the early, nuclear 40S trans-acting factor NOC4L was not detected.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data analyzed by immunoblotting.

claim: The early, nuclear 40S trans-acting factor NOC4L was not detected in USP16 tandem affinity purification.
source: This confirmed that pre-40S subunits were co-purified with both WT and mutant USP16-StHA as indicated by the presence of the late 40S trans-acting factor NOB1 and the 40S RP RPS3/uS3, whereas the early, nuclear 40S trans-acting factor NOC4L was not detected.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data analyzed by immunoblotting.

claim: The 60S trans-acting factor RLP24 and the ribosomal protein RPL23a/uL23 were absent in USP16 tandem affinity purification.
source: The absence of the 60S trans-acting factor RLP24 and the ribosomal protein RPL23a/uL23 further confirmed that USP16 specifically binds to 40S precursors.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data analyzed by immunoblotting.

claim: RPS10/eS10 was detected in the USP16 tandem affinity purification eluate.
source: Notably, the small ribosomal subunit protein RPS10/eS10 was also detected in the eluate.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data.

claim: RPS10 has been suggested to stably join pre-40S subunits at a very late cytoplasmic step of 40S maturation.
source: RPS10 has previously been suggested to stably join pre-40S subunits at a very late cytoplasmic step of 40S maturation, since it is not detected in earlier pre-40S particles purified by TAP of LTV1 or C21ORF70, a nuclear 40S assembly factor, or by Rio2 TAP from yeast (Collins et al., 2018; Larburu et al., 2016; Strunk et al., 2011; Zemp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The presence of RPS10 in USP16-associated 40S particles indicates that USP16 is associated with particles corresponding to pre-40S subunits at a very late stage of cytoplasmic maturation.
source: The presence of RPS10 in USP16-associated 40S particles thus indicates that USP16 is associated with particles corresponding to pre-40S subunits at a very late stage of cytoplasmic maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of RPS10 and prior knowledge about its assembly timing.

claim: USP16 contains an N-terminal zinc-finger ubiquitin binding domain (ZnF-UBP) domain.
source: USP16, in addition to its USP domain, contains an N-terminal zinc-finger ubiquitin binding domain (ZnF-UBP) domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statement about the domain structure of USP16 shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The USP domain of USP16 contains an insertion of approximately 200 amino acids not found in other members of the USP family except for USP45.
source: The USP domain itself contains an insertion of approximately 200 amino acids (aa), which is not found in other members of the USP family except for USP45, the most closely related DUB of USP16 in vertebrates (Clague et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The isolated ZnF domain associated with pre-40S particles, although their enrichment was slightly diminished compared to the WT.
source: The isolated ZnF domain associated with pre-40S particles, although their enrichment was slightly diminished compared to the WT, especially considering the higher expression levels of the ZnF domain.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Binding of pre-40S subunits to the USP domain was strongly compromised.
source: In contrast, binding of pre-40S subunits to the USP domain was strongly compromised and only very low levels were detectable both by silver staining and immunoblotting.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Deletion of the USP16-specific basic helix (ΔH) did not alter binding to pre-40S subunits compared to full-length USP16.
source: Further, deletion of the USP16-specific basic helix (ΔH) did not alter binding to pre-40S subunits compared to full-length USP16.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The weak 40S association of the isolated USP domain was completely lost upon deletion of the basic helix.
source: However, the weak 40S association of the isolated USP domain was completely lost upon deletion of the basic helix.
evidence: This is based on tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Mainly the ZnF domain but also the positively charged helix within the USP domain contribute to pre-40S binding.
source: Taken together, we conclude that mainly the ZnF domain but also the positively charged helix within the USP domain contribute to pre-40S binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the domain deletion experiments.

claim: Several RPs of the 40S subunit have been linked to ubiquitination.
source: Several RPs of the 40S subunit have been linked to ubiquitination and are thus candidate USP16 substrates. For instance, RPS2/uS5, RPS3/uS3, RPS3a/eS1, RPS10/eS10, and RPS20/uS10 contain sites for regulatory mono-ubiquitination (Garzia et al., 2017; Higgins et al., 2015; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RPS27a/eS31 is produced as a linear fusion with ubiquitin (Ub), which is cleaved off before the ribosome reaches translation competence.
source: Furthermore, the ribosomal protein RPS27a/eS31 is produced as a linear fusion with ubiquitin (Ub), which is cleaved off before the ribosome reaches translation competence (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Knockdown of USP16 with two different siRNAs led to the appearance of a higher molecular weight band of RPS27a.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of USP16 with two different siRNAs led to the appearance of a higher molecular weight band of RPS27a, but not of the other ribosomal proteins tested.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Depletion of USP16 in either parental HEK293 cells or in uninduced USP16 cell lines led to the appearance of a higher molecular weight band of RPS27a.
source: As observed before, depletion of USP16 in either parental HEK293 cells or in uninduced USP16 cell lines led to the appearance of a higher molecular weight band of RPS27a.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The appearance of the higher molecular weight band of RPS27a upon USP16 depletion could be rescued by tetracycline-induced expression of tagged WT but not mutant USP16.
source: Importantly, this could be rescued by tetracycline-induced expression of tagged WT but not mutant USP16, indicating that the catalytic activity of USP16 is required for removal of the RPS27a modification.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The catalytic activity of USP16 is required for removal of the RPS27a modification.
source: Importantly, this could be rescued by tetracycline-induced expression of tagged WT but not mutant USP16, indicating that the catalytic activity of USP16 is required for removal of the RPS27a modification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment results.

claim: StrepTactin affinity purification of mutant USP16 co-purified modified RPS27a even in presence of endogenous USP16.
source: Interestingly, StrepTactin affinity purification of mutant USP16 co-purified modified RPS27a even in presence of endogenous USP16 (Figure 4E), suggesting that catalytically inactive USP16 acts in a dominant-negative manner on removal of the RPS27a modification.
evidence: This is based on affinity purification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Catalytically inactive USP16 acts in a dominant-negative manner on removal of the RPS27a modification.
source: Interestingly, StrepTactin affinity purification of mutant USP16 co-purified modified RPS27a even in presence of endogenous USP16 (Figure 4E), suggesting that catalytically inactive USP16 acts in a dominant-negative manner on removal of the RPS27a modification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-purification data.

claim: USP16 KO in both HeLa and HEK293 cell lines recapitulated the increase in RPS27a modification observed upon USP16 depletion.
source: USP16 KO in both HeLa and HEK293 cell lines recapitulated the increase in RPS27a modification observed upon USP16 depletion (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from USP16 KO cell lines shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Tetracycline-induced expression of WT but not mutant USP16-StHA in the HEK293 USP16 KO background could rescue the USP16 KO and led to a decrease of modified RPS27a.
source: Importantly, tetracycline-induced expression of WT but not mutant USP16-StHA in the HEK293 USP16 KO background could rescue the USP16 KO and led to a decrease of modified RPS27a (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Denaturing immunoprecipitation revealed an overlay of the modified RPS27a band with the Ub band, indicating that depletion of USP16 leads to an accumulation of a mono-ubiquitinated form of RPS27a.
source: This revealed an overlay of the modified RPS27a band with the Ub band, indicating that depletion of USP16 leads to an accumulation of a mono-ubiquitinated form of RPS27a (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on denaturing immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treating USP16 KO cells with MG132 for 2 or 4 hr led to a strong decrease of modified RPS27a.
source: Treating USP16 KO cells with MG132 for 2 or 4 hr indeed led to a strong decrease of modified RPS27a (Figure 5B), hinting at a regulatory role of RPS27a mono-ubiquitination.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from MG132 treatment experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The decrease of modified RPS27a upon MG132 treatment hints at a regulatory role of RPS27a mono-ubiquitination.
source: Treating USP16 KO cells with MG132 for 2 or 4 hr indeed led to a strong decrease of modified RPS27a (Figure 5B), hinting at a regulatory role of RPS27a mono-ubiquitination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MG132 treatment results.

claim: Seven Lys residues (K89, K90, K96, K99, K107, K113, K152) in RPS27a are solvent-exposed and not directly involved in rRNA binding.
source: Seven Lys residues (K89, K90, K96, K99, K107, K113, K152) are, however, solvent-exposed and not directly involved in rRNA binding (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When USP16 was depleted in cell lines expressing a C-terminally StHA-tagged RPS27a construct harboring mutations of seven lysines to arginine (RPS27a(7R)-StHA), ubiquitination was no longer observed.
source: Indeed, when we depleted USP16 in cell lines expressing a C-terminally StHA-tagged RPS27a construct harboring these mutations (RPS27a(7R)-StHA), ubiquitination was no longer observed, whereas the WT construct was still modified (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from experiments with mutant RPS27a shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ubiquitination was reestablished when Lys113 was re-introduced in the RPS27a(6R(K113))-StHA construct.
source: To pinpoint the exact modification site, we individually reverted the mutated residues to Lys and observed that ubiquitination was reestablished when Lys113 was re-introduced (RPS27a(6R(K113))-StHA).
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from experiments with mutant RPS27a shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mutation of Lys113 to Arg (Rps27a(K113R)-StHA) abolished RPS27a ubiquitination upon USP16 depletion.
source: We confirmed Lys113 as the sole modification site by its mutation to Arg (Rps27a(K113R)-StHA), which indeed abolished RPS27a ubiquitination upon USP16 depletion.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data from experiments with mutant RPS27a shown in Figure 5D.

claim: USP16 functions as a DUB for RPS27a, trans-mono-ubiquitinated on Lys113.
source: Together, our data show that USP16 functions as a DUB for RPS27a, trans-mono-ubiquitinated on Lys113.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis and rescue experiments.

claim: A striking increase of the 18S-E rRNA precursor was observed in USP16 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, while early rRNA precursors seemed unaffected in USP16 KO cells, we observed a striking increase of the 18S-E rRNA precursor in USP16 KO cells indicating that USP16 deletion affects the final step of 18S rRNA processing, which is catalyzed by the endonuclease NOB1 in the cytoplasm (Fatica et al., 2003; Pertschy et al., 2009; Preti et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on Northern blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: USP16 deletion affects the final step of 18S rRNA processing, which is catalyzed by the endonuclease NOB1 in the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, while early rRNA precursors seemed unaffected in USP16 KO cells, we observed a striking increase of the 18S-E rRNA precursor in USP16 KO cells indicating that USP16 deletion affects the final step of 18S rRNA processing, which is catalyzed by the endonuclease NOB1 in the cytoplasm (Fatica et al., 2003; Pertschy et al., 2009; Preti et al., 2013; Sloan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Northern blot data and supported by citations.

claim: ENP1 localization was not affected in HeLa USP16 KO cells.
source: While ENP1 localization was not affected in HeLa USP16 KO cells (Figure 6C, upper panel), DIM2 partially relocalized to the cytoplasm, suggesting a cytoplasmic 40S maturation defect that does not affect the release of ENP1 but that of DIM2 from 40S subunits in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DIM2 partially relocalized to the cytoplasm in HeLa USP16 KO cells.
source: While ENP1 localization was not affected in HeLa USP16 KO cells (Figure 6C, upper panel), DIM2 partially relocalized to the cytoplasm, suggesting a cytoplasmic 40S maturation defect that does not affect the release of ENP1 but that of DIM2 from 40S subunits in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The expression of transiently transfected WT but not mutant USP16-StHA rescued the late 40S biogenesis defect and restored nuclear localization of DIM2.
source: Importantly, the expression of transiently transfected WT but not mutant USP16-StHA rescued the late 40S biogenesis defect and restored nuclear localization of DIM2 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Both NOB1 and RIOK1 showed enhanced cytoplasmic localization in LMB-treated USP16 KO cells.
source: Strikingly, both NOB1 and RIOK1 showed enhanced cytoplasmic localization in LMB-treated USP16 KO cells indicating an inhibition of their release from cytoplasmic pre-40S subunits (Figure 6C, lower panel).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The enhanced cytoplasmic localization of NOB1 and RIOK1 in USP16 KO cells was reverted by expression of WT but not mutant USP16-StHA.
source: For both factors, the phenotype was reverted by expression of WT but not mutant USP16-StHA (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: USP16 deletion only affects very late stages of cytoplasmic pre-40S maturation, after release of ENP1 and before or during release of DIM2, NOB1, and RIOK1.
source: Together, these data indicate that USP16 deletion only affects very late stages of cytoplasmic pre-40S maturation, after release of ENP1 and before or during release of DIM2, NOB1, and RIOK1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data of various assembly factors.

claim: Treatment of HeLa WT and USP16 KO cells with actinomycin D did not lead to a change in the levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a.
source: Therefore, we treated HeLa WT and USP16 KO cells with a low dose of actinomycin D to specifically inhibit RNA polymerase I and thereby block ribosome assembly. This, however, did not lead to a change in the levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a (Figure 7, Supporting Figure 1), which may indicate that (pre-)40S subunits with mono-ubiquitinated RPS27a have a low turnover rate that exceeds the duration of the actinomycin D treatment or that ubiquitination of RPS27a might not be strictly dependent on ribosome maturation, for instance by also affecting mature subunits.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7, Supporting Figure 1.

claim: Ubiquitinated RPS27a was found in fractions containing (pre-)40S subunits, 80S ribosomes and polysomes to the same extent.
source: Interestingly, ubiquitinated RPS27a, like its unmodified form, was found in fractions containing (pre-)40S subunits, 80S ribosomes and polysomes to the same extent, suggesting that ubiquitination of RPS27a on (pre-)40S subunits does not hinder them from associating with mRNAs and entering the translating ribosome pool.
evidence: This is based on sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ubiquitination of RPS27a on (pre-)40S subunits does not hinder them from associating with mRNAs and entering the translating ribosome pool.
source: Interestingly, ubiquitinated RPS27a, like its unmodified form, was found in fractions containing (pre-)40S subunits, 80S ribosomes and polysomes to the same extent, suggesting that ubiquitination of RPS27a on (pre-)40S subunits does not hinder them from associating with mRNAs and entering the translating ribosome pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sucrose gradient data.

claim: An imbalance in the amount of free 40S and 60S subunits was observed in USP16 KO cells with a slight decrease in the amount of free 40S and a striking increase in the amount of free 60S subunits.
source: As expected, based on our previous observations that deletion of USP16 leads to a 40S biogenesis defect, we observed an imbalance in the amount of free 40S and 60S subunits with a slight decrease in the amount of free 40S and a striking increase in the amount of free 60S subunits in USP16 KO cells.
evidence: This is based on polysome profile data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Polysome levels were slightly decreased while the 80S peak was substantially larger in USP16 KO cells.
source: In addition, polysome levels were slightly decreased while the 80S peak was substantially larger, which is reminiscent of changes in polysome profiles due to a translation initiation defect or different stress conditions leading to polysome disassembly and a concomitant increase of 80S monosomes (Coudert et al., 2014; Kressler et al., 1997; Lacombe et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on polysome profile data shown in Figure 7B and supported by citations.

claim: USP16 deletion leads to ribosomes having some defect in translation.
source: Thus, our data indicate that USP16 deletion leads to ribosomes having some defect in translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polysome profile data.

claim: The levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a in USP16 KO cells were significantly decreased after treatment with cycloheximide.
source: Whereas no changes were observed after treatment of WT cells, the levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a in USP16 KO cells were significantly decreased after treatment with CHX or upon inhibition of translation initiation by silvestrol or DTT, suggesting that RPS27a ubiquitination is dependent on active translation.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a in USP16 KO cells were significantly decreased upon inhibition of translation initiation by silvestrol or DTT.
source: Whereas no changes were observed after treatment of WT cells, the levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a in USP16 KO cells were significantly decreased after treatment with CHX or upon inhibition of translation initiation by silvestrol or DTT, suggesting that RPS27a ubiquitination is dependent on active translation.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RPS27a ubiquitination is dependent on active translation.
source: Whereas no changes were observed after treatment of WT cells, the levels of ubiquitinated RPS27a in USP16 KO cells were significantly decreased after treatment with CHX or upon inhibition of translation initiation by silvestrol or DTT, suggesting that RPS27a ubiquitination is dependent on active translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the translation inhibition experiments.

claim: Treatment of cells with G418 led to a significant increase in the level of ubiquitinated RPS27a in HeLa USP16 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, when we treated cells with G418, we observed a significant increase in the level of ubiquitinated RPS27a in HeLa USP16 KO cells (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: G418 binds to the decoding center of the ribosome and induces A-site miscoding thereby decreasing translational fidelity.
source: G418 binds to the decoding center of the ribosome and induces A-site miscoding thereby decreasing translational fidelity and promoting missense errors during protein synthesis including premature termination codon readthrough (Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2014; Howard et al., 1996; Manuvakhova et al., 2000; Prokhorova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: USP16 localizes primarily to the cytoplasm of cultured human somatic cells.
source: Although USP16 has been shown to localize to chromosomes in mitotic cells and catalytically inactive USP16 has been reported to accumulate in the nucleus of interphase cells after prolonged expression (Cai et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2014), we and others have observed that USP16 localizes primarily to the cytoplasm of cultured human somatic cells (Cai et al., 1999; Sen Nkwe et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the study's data and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lys113 of RPS27a is conserved in S. cerevisiae but not S. pombe.
source: Interestingly, while Lys113 of RPS27a is conserved in S. cerevisiae but not S. pombe, USP16 and also its most closely related DUB USP45 are not conserved in yeast (Clague et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: USP16 and its most closely related DUB USP45 are not conserved in yeast.
source: Interestingly, while Lys113 of RPS27a is conserved in S. cerevisiae but not S. pombe, USP16 and also its most closely related DUB USP45 are not conserved in yeast (Clague et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Co-depletion of ZNF598 with USP16 did not induce changes in the ubiquitination levels of RPS27a.
source: Notably, in contrast to most of the other described regulatory mono-ubiquitination sites on the 40S subunit that reside in protruding flexible tails of ribosomal proteins, Lys113 resides in a part of RPS27a that is closely annealed to the surface of the 40S subunit. In fact, co-depletion of ZNF598 with USP16 did not induce changes in the ubiquitination levels of RPS27a (Figure 7, Supporting Figure 2), indicating that ZNF598 may not be the responsible E3 ligase.
evidence: This is based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7, Supporting Figure 2.

claim: ZNF598 may not be the E3 ligase responsible for RPS27a ubiquitination.
source: Notably, in contrast to most of the other described regulatory mono-ubiquitination sites on the 40S subunit that reside in protruding flexible tails of ribosomal proteins, Lys113 resides in a part of RPS27a that is closely annealed to the surface of the 40S subunit. In fact, co-depletion of ZNF598 with USP16 did not induce changes in the ubiquitination levels of RPS27a (Figure 7, Supporting Figure 2), indicating that ZNF598 may not be the responsible E3 ligase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-depletion experiment.

claim: Only about a fifth of the RPS27a pool is mono-ubiquitinated in USP16 KO cells.
source: The fact that only about a fifth of the RPS27a pool is mono-ubiquitinated in USP16 KO cells could indicate that the modification is restricted to a subset of (pre-)40S particles.
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunoblotting data.

claim: Analysis of the ubiquitin-modified proteome has identified Lys113 of RPS27a as a ubiquitination site in HCT116 cells.
source: Interestingly, while we do not observe mono-ubiquitinated RPS27a in WT cells by immunoblotting, analysis of the ubiquitin-modified proteome has identified Lys113 of RPS27a as a ubiquitination site in HCT116 cells (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Lys113 will not be obscured by binding of the 60S subunit and should not interfere with ongoing translation.
source: Lys113 will not be obscured by binding of the 60S subunit and should not interfere with ongoing translation as no translation factors have so far been mapped to this area of the ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge of the ribosome.

claim: USP16 is only enriched in the (pre-)40S peak of sucrose gradients.
source: Mono-ubiquitinated RPS27a is indeed found in fractions of sucrose gradients containing (pre-)40S subunits, 80S ribosomes and polysomes, whereas USP16 is only enriched in the (pre-)40S peak.
evidence: This is based on sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 7A.

claim: USP16 might only be able to bind and deubiquitinate free (pre-)40S subunits.
source: Thus, USP16 might only be able to bind and deubiquitinate free (pre-)40S subunits while ubiquitinated (pre-)40S particles can enter the pool of translating ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sedimentation behavior of USP16 and ubiquitinated RPS27a.

claim: Deletion of USP16 leads to a slight decrease in polysome levels and a striking increase of the 80S peak.
source: In support of such a hypothesis, deletion of USP16 leads to a slight decrease in polysome levels and a striking increase of the 80S peak, which is commonly interpreted as a translation initiation defect (e.g. Coudert et al., 2014; Kressler et al., 1997; Lacombe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on polysome profile data and supported by citations.

claim: RPS27a mono-ubiquitination is strongly and rapidly diminished upon inhibition of translation in USP16 knockout cells.
source: RPS27a mono-ubiquitination is strongly and rapidly diminished upon inhibition of translation in USP16 knockout cells.
evidence: This is based on the translation inhibition experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The loss of RPS27a mono-ubiquitination upon inhibition of translation initiation suggests that the modification may occur only after mRNA association.
source: The loss of RPS27a mono-ubiquitination upon inhibition of translation initiation also suggests that the modification may occur only after mRNA association.
evidence: This is an inference based on the translation inhibition experiments.
